title: Generative AI use in K-12 education: a systematic review
extended_summary:
This paper reviews empirical research on generative AI (GenAI) use in K-12 education, focusing on how GenAI has been used, in what contexts, and with what reported impacts. The author conducted a systematic review using Scopus and Web of Science plus snowballing, screening papers against inclusion criteria that required empirical use of GenAI in teaching or learning within K-12 or closely related vocational settings.

Across 30 included papers, the review finds that GenAI work in K-12 has concentrated on high school and pre-service teachers, with much less attention to in-service teachers, elementary grades, or special populations. ChatGPT was by far the dominant tool, although some studies used Midjourney, Copilot, Canva, and custom GenAI-based tools. Subject coverage skewed strongly toward STEM, especially mathematics and physics, but also included programming, science, writing, English, history, and AI-related activities.

The review concludes that quasi-experimental designs are the most common, but that the evidence base relies heavily on self-reported outcomes such as attitudes, trust, self-efficacy, and engagement rather than objective learning measures. It also notes that teacher professional development is frequently recommended, yet actual studies involving in-service teachers, instructional practice, parent involvement, rural settings, and long-term or rigorous classroom evaluation remain sparse. The paper argues that future work should examine real-time classroom use, broader subject areas, and better outcome measures to support effective GenAI integration in schools.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools or chatbots used for educational content generation, assistance, and feedback tasks in K-12 settings.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a systematic review of empirical K-12 studies using GenAI tools; it synthesizes how tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot, Midjourney, and others were used across subjects, grade bands, and settings.

findings.finding_summary: Across 30 included studies, the review found that most existing work focused on high school and preservice teachers, with middle school also represented; in-service teachers were barely targeted. Subject coverage was concentrated in STEM, especially mathematics and physics, while non-STEM areas such as writing and English were less common. The review also notes a lack of evidence in early childhood, special needs, and rural contexts, and very limited work involving instructional coaches or teacher professional development beyond general calls for training.
findings.measure: Distribution of included studies by educational level, subject area, country/context, and study design

quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review synthesizing heterogeneous primary studies rather than a single controlled evaluation. The evidence is informative but largely descriptive and based on the included studies' varied designs and measures.
impact_tier_rationale: The review indicates clear patterns of use and gaps, but it does not report a pooled causal effect size. The practical impact is therefore suggestive rather than quantitatively established.
